summary: Genesis tells of origins: of the world, of humanity and of the people of Israel. Chapters 1 to 11 narrate the creation, the disobedience in the garden of Eden, the flood and the scattering of the peoples at Babel. From chapter 12 on, the story focuses on one family: Abraham receives from God the promise of land, descendants and blessing, and this promise passes to Isaac, to Jacob and to Jacob's twelve sons. The book ends with the family living in Egypt, which sets the stage for Exodus.
name: The name “Genesis” comes from Greek and means “origin”; it is the title the book received in the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible. In Hebrew the book is called Bereshit, “In the beginning,” which is its first word.

structure.title: Origins of the world and of humanity
structure.text: Creation, Eden, Cain and Abel, the genealogies, the flood, the covenant with Noah and the tower of Babel.

structure.title: Abraham
structure.text: The call, the promise, the covenant and the birth of Isaac.

structure.title: Isaac and Jacob
structure.text: Esau and Jacob, the blessing, Jacob's years with Laban and the new name, Israel.

structure.title: Joseph
structure.text: Sold by his brothers, Joseph rises to governor of Egypt and is reunited with his family.

extra.title: The generations (toledot)
extra.text: The book is organized around a formula repeated about ten times: “this is the account (or the generations) of…”, in Hebrew toledot. It opens each new stage of the story, from 2:4 to 37:2.

writing.tradition: Jewish and Christian traditions attribute the Torah to Moses. On this reading, Genesis would have been written during the wandering in the wilderness, around 1446–1406 BC, or in the 13th century BC for those who adopt a later date for the Exodus.
writing.academic: Most scholars understand that the book brings together oral and written traditions from different periods, edited over centuries. The final form is usually dated to the periods of the Babylonian exile and Persian rule, around 550–400 BC.

events.intro: Chapters 1 to 11 narrate origins and give no dates that history can place. For Abraham and his descendants, a traditional chronology adds up the ages and intervals given in the text itself and places the Exodus around 1446 BC; its result is what appears on the timeline. There are no records outside the Bible that mention the patriarchs, and many historians consider these narratives impossible to date; those who place them usually point to the Middle Bronze Age, from about 2000 to 1550 BC.

context: The stories of Genesis take place in the ancient Near East, between Mesopotamia and Egypt. Abraham sets out from Ur of the Chaldeans, in southern Mesopotamia, passes through Haran and goes on to Canaan; later, Joseph brings the family to the region of Goshen, in Egypt. Scholars compare the first chapters with older Mesopotamian texts, such as the Enuma Elish, about creation, and the epics of Atrahasis and Gilgamesh, which also tell of a great flood. The similarities and the differences help us see what the biblical text affirms about God and human beings.
